title: The Colportage Association: The Network of Christian Book Distributors on the Streets
description: Discover how the Metropolitan Tabernacle Colportage Association and Susannah Spurgeon

content.text: The Power of the Printed Page

Charles Haddon Spurgeon understood that while his powerful voice could command the attention of thousands within the walls of the Metropolitan Tabernacle, the printed page possessed the unique ability to transcend geographical boundaries and enter the homes of those who would never attend a church service. To combat the rising tide of cheap, secular, and often heterodox literature circulating in Victorian England, Spurgeon realized the absolute necessity of a mobilized, grassroots force of literature distributors who could bring the truth directly to the people.
The Foundation of the Colportage Association

In direct connection with the evangelistic zeal generated by the Pastors' College, the Metropolitan Tabernacle Colportage Association was established. The colporteurs were essentially traveling evangelists and book salesmen who walked the streets, visiting rural villages, country lanes, and urban slums alike. Their primary mission was the evangelization and distribution of sound theological material. They sold Bibles, good Puritan books, and Spurgeon's own printed sermons at highly affordable prices, while also distributing free gospel tracts to the poorest citizens.

These men were not merely traveling merchants; they were frontline missionaries. As they went from house to house, they engaged individuals in personal conversations about their souls and the Gospel of Jesus Christ. The association grew steadily and proved to be a highly effective evangelistic machine. By the year 1891, the Colportage Association employed 96 active colporteurs spreading the Gospel throughout the country. Through this vast network, Spurgeon ensured that the working-class people of England had access to literature that would edify their souls and point them to the Savior.

Complementing this massive effort of grassroots literature distribution was the extraordinary and highly impactful work of Spurgeon's wife, Susannah. Recognizing that many rural pastors and nonconformist ministers were too impoverished to afford the theological books necessary for their own pastoral study and sermon preparation, Susannah inaugurated the "Book Fund" in 1875.

Despite suffering from severe gynecological health issues that required surgery in 1869 and left her as a virtual invalid for the remainder of her life, Susannah tirelessly managed this charity directly from her home. Her unwavering support for her husband's ministry and her commitment to the glory of God drove her to supply impoverished ministers with robust theological libraries. By the time of her death in October 1903, the Book Fund had successfully distributed an astonishing 200,000 theological books to needy pastors across the nation.

Through the Colportage Association reaching the common people on the streets, and Susannah's Book Fund equipping the shepherds in the pulpits, the Spurgeons ensured that robust, Reformed, and Puritan theology saturated the British landscape. They practically demonstrated that a well-read congregation and a well-equipped, biblically grounded ministry were the greatest bulwarks against the theological decline of their era.
